prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: GCS 9, below 10, is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because GCS is 9 (E2 V3 M4), below 10 (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours, or benzylpenicillin for the penicillin-susceptible isolate (MIC 0.06 mg/L), for 14 days (NICE NG240).

Request neurosurgical assessment of the VP shunt, including a shunt reservoir tap for cell count, Gram stain and culture, to decide whether the shunt is involved and needs externalisation or removal (IDSA 2017).
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
After recovery, investigate this second episode of pneumococcal meningitis for a cranial CSF leak and for immunodeficiency, and offer pneumococcal vaccination.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because GCS is 9, below 10 (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Chronic deficits documented at baseline (here the left spastic hemiparesis and extensor plantar from neonatal meningitis) are not new focal signs; the imaging criterion in this patient is the depressed GCS.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Shunt-associated meningitis must be distinguished from community-acquired bacterial meningitis; coagulase-negative staphylococci and Cutibacterium acnes are the dominant shunt organisms. In community-acquired meningitis the ventricular CSF of a shunted patient is also inflamed, usually less than the lumbar CSF; whether the shunt must be externalised or removed is a neurosurgical decision (IDSA 2017).
A second episode of pneumococcal meningitis is recurrent bacterial meningitis and calls for a search for a cranial CSF leak and for immunodeficiency.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Pneumococcal meningitis can occur in shunted patients and is treated as community-acquired pneumococcal meningitis (ceftriaxone with dexamethasone); shunt assessment proceeds in parallel (IDSA 2017).

red_herrings.intended_effect: Narrow empiric coverage to shunt organisms (CoNS) and delay broader community-acquired coverage.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilloedema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: GCS 9 (E2 V3 M4), below 10; the left hemiparesis and extensor plantar are chronic and are not new focal signs. NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (intracranial shunt). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ricardo Fuentes is a 38-year-old right-handed man who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after his wife found him increasingly confused and febrile at home. He has a significant past medical history of neonatal pneumococcal meningitis complicated by hydrocephalus requiring ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement in infancy, with a single shunt revision during adolescence. He has a residual mild left-sided spastic hemiparesis but is functionally independent in all activities of daily living and works full-time as a warehouse logistics supervisor. Yesterday morning, approximately 18 hours before presentation, the patient developed a frontal headache that he initially attributed to his chronic tension headaches. He took his usual ibuprofen without relief. By the afternoon, his wife noticed he felt warm and took his temperature, recording 38.6 degrees Celsius. He complained of worsening neck stiffness that he described as different from his usual headaches, specifically localized to the posterior neck and exacerbated by bending forward. He took acetaminophen and went to lie down in a dark room, complaining that the living room lights were causing intense pain. Overnight, his condition deteriorated rapidly. His wife heard him moaning and found him curled on his side, drenched in sweat, and mumbling incoherently. He was unable to recognize their daughter and became agitated when she tried to sit him up. He vomited three times between midnight and early morning. By 05:00 this morning, he was barely responsive to verbal commands. His wife called 911 when she was unable to rouse him from bed. Paramedics recorded a temperature of 39.9 degrees Celsius en route and noted significant neck rigidity during assessment. His wife reports no recent sick contacts with meningitis, no recent dental procedures, and no trauma to the head or shunt site. She notes he had a mild upper respiratory infection with nasal congestion approximately ten days ago that resolved on its own. She is unsure of his pneumococcal vaccination status but believes he received childhood vaccinations. There has been no seizure activity witnessed, no new rashes, and no recent changes in shunt function.
